An income percentage needs its dollar cap: review disability cover as eligible earnings change

Use four charts to apply a hypothetical monthly benefit cap, compare possible future claim-start reviews and distinguish a gross income percentage from actual household cash protection.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Read a hypothetical income percentage beside its monthly dollar cap

Interactive planning lab

Starting monthly gross amount under the hypothetical formula$4,000
Starting formula amount divided by eligible gross earnings50.00%
Final-review formula amount divided by that review’s eligible gross earnings33.78%

Original hypothetical formula, not an insurance quote or a benefit determination. At each review, a possible new eligible claim would receive the smaller of the stated percentage of eligible monthly gross earnings and the fixed monthly gross dollar cap. Eligibility and payment are assumed only to illustrate that arithmetic. Eligible earnings rise at the selected constant rate before each separate possible claim-start date; the percentage and cap stay unchanged. The sequence is not a payment path for one ongoing disability claim, and it does not add salary and insurance as concurrent receipts. All values are nominal gross amounts before any applicable tax. Actual definitions of insured earnings, disability, claim approval, benefit offsets, tax, waiting periods, duration, indexation, premiums and coverage amendments are excluded. The formula ratio is not a comparison of net take-home income and is not an assessment that household expenses are covered. Future earnings and unchanged policy terms are assumptions, not forecasts or insurer commitments.

The central idea

A stated income percentage and a maximum monthly amount work together. Once the dollar cap binds, the formula can represent a smaller share of rising eligible earnings.

01

Read the percentage and the maximum as one formula

A phrase such as “60% of earnings” does not establish a monthly payment on its own. A dollar maximum can limit the result, and the plan’s definition of eligible earnings determines the amount to which the percentage applies.

The FCAC disability-insurance guide describes income replacement up to a maximum amount for a specified period. It also highlights monthly payment amounts, tax treatment, waiting periods and other plan terms as items to understand.

The charts use an invented formula: take the smaller of a percentage of eligible monthly gross earnings and a fixed monthly gross cap. No actual policy, approval rule or insurer quotation is reproduced.

02

Calculate the starting gross ratio after the cap

The default example treats CAD 8,000 of monthly gross earnings as eligible. At 60%, the percentage calculation produces CAD 4,800. The invented monthly maximum is CAD 4,000, so the formula is reduced by CAD 800.

The resulting CAD 4,000 is 50% of the eligible CAD 8,000, even though the formula’s percentage component is 60%. The waterfall makes both stages visible.

If eligible monthly earnings were CAD 5,000 under the same terms, 60% would produce CAD 3,000. That is below the CAD 4,000 cap, so the formula would remain CAD 3,000, or 60% of those eligible earnings.

03

Treat each future point as a separate possible claim-start date

The default review path assumes eligible monthly earnings rise by 4% a year while the percentage and dollar cap remain fixed. After ten years, the modeled eligible earnings are about CAD 11,841.95 a month.

The percentage calculation would then exceed the unchanged CAD 4,000 cap. The gross formula amount is still CAD 4,000, representing about 33.78% of the earnings assumed eligible at that later review.

This is a set of alternative claim-start scenarios. It does not show the payment path of one person already receiving disability benefits. A claim that began today would follow its own contract, including any applicable indexation and review rules; it would not automatically use the healthy-worker salary path drawn here.

04

Keep a gross replacement ratio separate from net cash available for bills

The chart divides the gross formula amount by eligible gross earnings. It does not calculate normal take-home pay or a benefit payment after tax. Those two net amounts may have different deductions and treatment.

It also does not subtract other income offsets. The FCAC guide explains that disability benefits can interact with other sources and that plan terms vary. Simply adding every possible benefit would not establish a reliable household receipt total.

A cash budget needs verified net amounts and payment dates, plus the expenses that continue during an interruption. The ratio alone cannot establish that rent, debt payments, care costs or saving commitments are covered.

05

Use the matrix to locate which limit is binding

The matrix changes eligible monthly earnings and the dollar cap while retaining the entered percentage. At lower earnings, several caps can produce the same percentage because none limits the formula. At higher earnings, the cap can determine the amount instead.

With the default 60% component, CAD 4,000 of eligible earnings produces a CAD 2,400 formula amount under every displayed cap. CAD 16,000 of eligible earnings with a CAD 3,000 cap instead produces an 18.75% gross ratio.

These are formula comparisons, not competing product offers. They do not compare premiums, disability definitions, benefit periods, exclusions or underwriting. An arithmetic increase in a cap is not evidence that coverage can be increased on those terms.

06

Update the coverage record when the underlying earnings change

For an actual review, identify the earnings the policy counts, its percentage schedule, monthly maximum and other applicable limits. Record the possible benefit after offsets and tax using the actual policy and circumstances, rather than substituting this illustration.

Then place that amount on a cash calendar that includes the waiting period and any end date. The linked guides examine those timing questions and the different role of a lump-sum illness payment.

The purpose of the four charts is to expose the cap’s effect before a percentage becomes a household planning assumption. They do not determine a claim, forecast future policy terms or recommend a coverage amount.
